name_en: Love Cake (Sri Lankan Cashew Semolina Cake)

ingredients.name: Raw cashew nuts
ingredients.notes: dry-toasted and then coarsely ground in a food processor; do not grind to a paste -- the texture should be coarse and chunky

ingredients.name: Coarse semolina
ingredients.notes: dry-roasted in a pan until lightly golden, then mixed with melted butter while still hot

ingredients.name: Unsalted butter
ingredients.notes: melted and mixed into the hot roasted semolina

ingredients.name: Eggs
ingredients.notes: separated; yolks creamed with sugar, whites beaten to stiff peaks and folded in at the end

ingredients.name: Caster sugar
ingredients.notes: creamed with egg yolks until pale and thick

ingredients.name: Honey
ingredients.notes: bees honey preferred; adds moisture and a distinctive floral sweetness

ingredients.name: Rose water
ingredients.notes: essential to the cake's signature aroma; do not omit or substitute

ingredients.name: Lime
ingredients.notes: zest only; some recipes also use lemon zest

steps.instruction: Preheat the oven to 150C (300F). Line an 8-inch (20cm) square baking tin on all sides with a double layer of parchment paper, greasing between the layers -- this insulation prevents the exterior from overcooking while the interior reaches the right moist-chewy texture.

Dry-toast the semolina in a heavy pan over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, until it smells nutty and turns lightly golden, about 8-10 minutes. While still hot, immediately add the melted butter and mix well until the butter is fully absorbed. Set aside to cool to room temperature.
In a dry pan, lightly toast the cashews for 3-4 minutes until lightly coloured. Cool, then pulse in a food processor until coarsely ground -- small chunks remaining is correct. Set aside.
In a large bowl or stand mixer, beat the egg yolks with the sugar until the mixture is very pale, thick, and ribbony -- about 5-8 minutes with an electric mixer.
Add the honey, rose water, lime zest, cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, and salt to the creamed yolks. Mix well.
Add the coarsely ground cashews and fold in with a spatula. Then add the cooled semolina-butter mixture and fold in gently without beating.

In a clean bowl, beat the egg whites to firm glossy peaks using a clean whisk or mixer. Fold the beaten whites into the semolina-cashew batter in three additions, working gently to preserve as much air as possible.

Pour into the prepared tin and spread evenly. Bake at 150C for 60-75 minutes until the top is golden brown and a skewer inserted in the centre comes out with a few moist (not wet) crumbs attached. If the top browns too quickly, cover loosely with foil.

Cool completely in the tin before cutting. Love cake improves significantly over 2-3 days as the flavours deepen and meld. Serve in small squares dusted with icing sugar. Keeps for 2-3 weeks in an airtight tin.

source_site: 196flavors.com, cross-checked against ammiskitchennz.blogspot.com, nigella.com, thearmeniankitchen.com, tootingmama.com, everydaygourmet.tv, savoryspin.com, foodvoyageur.com, and Wikipedia (Love cake)
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 9+ independent sources; very strong agreement on the core flavour base (cashew, semolina, rose water, honey, lime zest) with natural household variation in exact ratios
notes: Love cake is considered Sri Lanka's most beloved and prestigious celebration cake, made for birthdays, Christmas, weddings, and almost every festive occasion in the Burgher community and beyond. The name is said to derive from the fact that grinding the spices and nuts makes it a 'labour of love', and locally it is rumoured that the cake was traditionally made by young women to give to suitors. Unlike bibikkan, love cake uses no coconut or jaggery -- it is defined by semolina, cashews, rose water, honey, and lime zest. The double-parchment lining of the tin is consistently recommended across sources and is important: the low 150C baking temperature and long bake time are necessary for the moist interior but can cause the exterior to over-brown without insulation. Rose water is non-negotiable and cannot be substituted; its floral aroma is the single most distinctive characteristic of the cake. Some recipes add candied pumpkin/winter melon preserve (puhul dosi) and/or a splash of brandy for extra richness -- both are authentic traditional additions.
